timeline.event: Construction began on the 40-story Hyatt Regency Kansas City.
The Hartford Civic Center roof collapsed amid a national pattern of notable structures failing at an alarming rate.
The Kemper Arena roof collapsed during a period when notable structures around the country were failing at an alarming rate.
The Hyatt Regency hotel officially opened.
The fourth-floor walkway dropped, paused, and collapsed onto the second-floor walkway, and both platforms fell onto a crowded tea dance in the lobby.
timeline.place: Hyatt Regency Hotel atrium lobby, Kansas City, Missouri

timeline.event: Architectural engineer Wayne G. Lischka and the firm Simpson, Gumpertz, and Heger Inc. were hired by The Kansas City Star to investigate the collapse and discovered a design change.
A laboratory at Lehigh University began testing box beams on behalf of the steel fabrication source within days of the collapse.
The Hyatt Regency reopened after its atrium was redesigned and a committee of engineers and architects found no other structural safety issues.
The Kansas City Star and the Kansas City Times won a Pulitzer Prize for their 16 months of investigative coverage of the collapse.
Local authorities reported that the $5 million hotel reconstruction made the building possibly the safest in the country.
The disaster was cited in an argument against the Reagan administration's attempt to eliminate an agency of the National Bureau of Standards.
Local rock band The Rainmakers memorialized the event in the song Rockin' at the T-Dance on their debut album.
The hotel was renamed the Hyatt Regency Crown Center.

legacy.what: The hotel atrium was redesigned, replacing the second-floor walkway with one supported by columns, permanently removing the other walkways, reinforcing the roof, and reopening the building.
The Kansas City Star and the Kansas City Times were awarded a Pulitzer Prize for their 16 months of investigative coverage of the collapse.
A $5 million hotel reconstruction was completed, leading local authorities to report the building as possibly the safest in the country.
The disaster was cited in arguments against the Reagan administration's attempt to eliminate an agency of the National Bureau of Standards.
The hotel was renamed the Hyatt Regency Crown Center.
